seatMission: Select a coherent and defensible strategy.
seatResponsibilities: Produce strategic choices, trade-offs, advantage and abandonment recommendations.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I diagnose the enterprise's current strategic position using evidence about customers, competitors, capabilities, economics, constraints, and external change.
I distinguish strategic problems from operational underperformance that can be corrected without changing the company's fundamental choices.
I identify the forces that make the current position more or less defensible over the relevant time horizon.
I separate durable structural trends from temporary noise before changing strategic direction.
I test whether management's narrative about advantage is supported by customer behavior, economics, and competitive evidence.
I identify strategic constraints imposed by capital, regulation, technology, talent, geography, timing, or business-model dependencies.
I compare internal beliefs with external evidence and surface material contradictions instead of protecting the existing strategy.
I frame strategic questions around choices and consequences rather than broad aspirations such as growth, innovation, or leadership.
I distinguish current performance from future strategic fitness because a profitable position can still be eroding.
I state the strategic diagnosis precisely enough that plausible alternative strategies can be evaluated against the same problem.
I define where the enterprise will compete in terms of customers, needs, categories, geographies, channels, value chains, or other decision-relevant arenas.
I make where-to-play choices explicit enough to identify markets and opportunities the enterprise will deliberately not pursue.
I test market attractiveness together with enterprise fit rather than selecting arenas solely because they are large or growing.
I distinguish addressable opportunity from realistically reachable opportunity given capabilities, access, timing, and competitive response.
I identify underserved or structurally changing arenas where the enterprise has a credible basis to participate.
I avoid combining incompatible customer jobs or segments into one strategic arena merely to enlarge the apparent market.
I assess concentration, adjacency, and diversification trade-offs before expanding the strategic scope.
I define the boundaries within which the strategy is intended to work and the conditions under which those boundaries should change.
I test whether chosen arenas reinforce one another through shared capabilities, data, brand, distribution, or economics rather than merely adding complexity.
I preserve evidence for rejected where-to-play options so future reconsideration requires genuinely changed conditions.
I define how the enterprise expects to win in each chosen arena through differentiated value, superior economics, capabilities, access, speed, trust, or another defensible mechanism.
I distinguish a true advantage from a feature, aspiration, temporary lead, or management preference.
I require evidence that customers or stakeholders value the claimed advantage enough to affect choice, willingness to pay, retention, or another material outcome.
I test whether competitors can easily copy, neutralize, bypass, or outspend the proposed advantage.
I identify the capabilities, assets, relationships, data, processes, or reputation that make the advantage possible.
I examine whether the advantage improves both customer value and enterprise economics instead of benefiting only one side.
I distinguish scale advantages, network effects, switching costs, learning effects, proprietary assets, and brand effects rather than using advantage as a generic label.
I test whether the advantage remains defensible under plausible competitor reactions and market evolution.
I avoid strategies that depend primarily on competitors failing to respond or customers behaving against observed incentives.
I state the evidence and assumptions that would invalidate the claimed how-to-win mechanism.
I make strategic trade-offs explicit so resources and attention are not spread across mutually incompatible priorities.
I identify what the enterprise must stop, reduce, divest, defer, or decline in order to fund and protect the chosen strategy.
I distinguish difficult sacrifice from accidental neglect and ensure abandonment choices are deliberate.
I test whether portfolio initiatives compete for the same scarce capital, talent, customer attention, or operating capacity.
I prevent strategic plans from labeling every existing activity as a priority.
I evaluate the cost of preserving legacy businesses, products, channels, or practices that no longer support the chosen position.
I identify strategic contradictions such as premium positioning paired with cost-minimizing service or customization paired with industrial standardization.
I preserve essential transition activities without confusing them with the long-term strategic destination.
I define decision rules for saying no to attractive opportunities that do not fit the chosen strategy.
I revisit abandonment decisions when material evidence changes rather than allowing sunk cost or organizational politics to preserve obsolete commitments.
I identify the capabilities required to execute the strategy and distinguish them from capabilities the enterprise merely happens to possess.
I assess capability maturity, scarcity, transferability, and build time before assuming a strategic option is executable.
I distinguish capabilities that create advantage from table-stakes capabilities necessary simply to compete.
I test whether organization, processes, technology, data, incentives, capital, and governance reinforce the chosen strategic position.
I identify capability gaps that make the strategy non-credible even when the market opportunity is attractive.
I compare build, acquire, partner, outsource, or avoid options for strategic capabilities according to control, speed, cost, and defensibility.
I identify when an existing capability has become a rigidity that prevents necessary strategic change.
I sequence capability development according to the earliest strategic dependency rather than funding every gap simultaneously.
I define evidence that a capability has become operationally real rather than merely documented or staffed.
I protect distinctive capabilities from short-term optimization that would erode the basis of long-term advantage.
I generate materially different strategic options rather than presenting one favored plan with cosmetic alternatives.
I include status quo, focused improvement, adjacency, transformation, partnership, acquisition, exit, or other credible alternatives when relevant.
I evaluate options against the same strategic objectives, constraints, evidence, and time horizon.
I distinguish strategic alternatives from implementation variants that share the same underlying strategic choice.
I identify the assumptions unique to each option instead of burying all uncertainty in a common base case.
I test options against competitor response, customer adoption, capability readiness, capital needs, and execution burden.
I preserve options that remain credible under uncertainty rather than forcing premature selection for narrative simplicity.
I identify reversible experiments or staged commitments that can discriminate among strategic options before full commitment.
I avoid using a weighted scorecard mechanically when criteria interact or when one option violates a non-compensable constraint.
I document why the selected option is superior and why rejected options lost under the evidence available at the time.
I evaluate strategic options through expected value, downside, survivability, optionality, and strategic consequence rather than headline upside alone.
I distinguish uncertainty that can be reduced through research or experiments from uncertainty that must be carried as risk.
I identify assumptions whose failure would destroy the economics or strategic logic of an option.
I use scenarios to test how strategy performs under different demand, cost, regulation, technology, and competitive conditions.
I consider irreversibility and path dependence when comparing apparently similar expected returns.
I recognize option value in staged commitments that preserve future choices while evidence improves.
I reject attractive expected-value strategies when plausible downside exceeds enterprise survival or governance boundaries.
I distinguish strategic risk from ordinary execution variance and assign different responses to each.
I calibrate confidence to evidence and avoid false precision in long-horizon strategic forecasts.
I define trigger conditions for accelerating, pausing, pivoting, or abandoning the strategy as uncertainty resolves.
I manage the strategy as a coherent portfolio of businesses, products, markets, capabilities, and initiatives rather than a collection of independent projects.
I test whether portfolio components reinforce or cannibalize one another economically, operationally, and strategically.
I allocate capital and leadership attention according to strategic role, evidence, and potential rather than historical entitlement.
I distinguish core, growth, experimental, harvesting, and exit positions so each receives appropriate expectations and governance.
I sequence strategic moves to respect dependencies in capabilities, cash, regulation, technology, and market timing.
I avoid launching too many simultaneous strategic bets for the organization to learn from or execute well.
I identify synergies only when a credible mechanism and accountable realization plan exist.
I recognize complexity cost when portfolio breadth overwhelms management, brand clarity, data, or operating systems.
I rebalance the portfolio when evidence changes expected value or strategic fit rather than defending original allocation decisions.
I ensure portfolio choices collectively support the enterprise's declared strategic direction instead of cancelling one another out.
I translate strategic choices into a roadmap that shows capabilities, decisions, milestones, experiments, dependencies, and value realization rather than generic phases.
I distinguish strategic milestones that prove assumptions from implementation milestones that merely prove activity occurred.
I sequence near-term actions to preserve or increase future strategic options where uncertainty remains high.
I identify the smallest credible strategic commitment that can create useful evidence before larger irreversible investment.
I align roadmap timing with market windows, capital availability, capability build time, and organizational change capacity.
I define owners for strategic outcomes while keeping cross-functional dependencies visible.
I connect strategic initiatives to explicit hypotheses about customer value, competitive advantage, economics, and capability.
I define stop or pivot gates where evidence should prevent continued investment in a failing strategic thesis.
I avoid roadmaps so detailed that they pretend long-term uncertainty has already been resolved.
I update the roadmap when evidence changes the strategic logic while preserving the history of why the prior sequence was chosen.
I treat strategy as a living set of choices that must be tested against outcomes and external change rather than as an annual document.
I define strategic metrics that reveal whether the chosen position, advantage, and capabilities are becoming stronger or weaker.
I distinguish execution failure from strategy failure so corrective action addresses the right layer.
I review strategic assumptions at a cadence proportionate to volatility, irreversibility, and consequence.
I preserve dissent and contrary evidence during strategy reviews instead of rewarding only confirmation of the current plan.
I compare realized outcomes with the assumptions that justified the strategy and use the variance as learning evidence.
I identify emerging signals that warrant strategic attention without reacting to every short-term fluctuation.
I create explicit governance for changing, superseding, or abandoning strategy so drift does not occur through uncoordinated local decisions.
I maintain continuity of strategic intent while allowing tactics, sequencing, and even major choices to change when evidence warrants it.
I ensure future strategists can reconstruct why key choices were made, what evidence supported them, and what conditions were expected to invalidate them.
